note: Finds GPT-4 guesses masked MMLU options 57 percent of the time, direct evidence of test set exposure in a closed model.
title: Investigating Data Contamination in Modern Benchmarks for Large Language Models
explain_beginner: This research discovered that GPT-4, a powerful AI system, has likely seen test questions before during its training. Researchers found that when they hid the correct answers to a famous benchmark test, GPT-4 could still guess the right options at much higher rates than expected by chance. This matters because it means we cannot trust benchmark scores as an accurate measure of the AI's true abilities if it has already encountered those questions.
explain_business: This finding reveals that benchmark scores reported for leading AI systems may not reflect genuine capability improvements, but rather exposure to test data. Organizations relying on published benchmarks to evaluate model quality or make procurement decisions should treat scores with skepticism. It highlights the need for contamination audits before deployment and suggests that truly novel evaluation methods are necessary to accurately compare AI systems.
explain_practitioner: The authors investigated data leakage in large language model benchmarks by analyzing whether models performed suspiciously well on masked test items. When presenting MMLU questions with hidden answer options, GPT-4 achieved 57 percent accuracy, significantly exceeding random baseline performance. This direct evidence suggests the model's training data included benchmark test sets, compromising the validity of standard evaluation metrics and indicating the need for stricter data contamination detection methods.
